student_passage:
Pieces of Morning

My alarm sounded before sunrise because I had promised my friend Lina that I would help install a mural beside the neighborhood train station. When we arrived, the wall held only a penciled grid. On the pavement, volunteers opened crates filled with small, tiny pieces[1] of blue, silver, and amber tile. I wondered how scraps no wider than my thumbnail could become anything recognizable.

The artist coordinating the project, Maya Chen, unrolled a paper plan and threw[2] its enlarged outline onto the wall with a portable projector. The pattern of numbered shapes were[3] confusing until she explained that each number corresponded to a crate. From across the courtyard, the design looked like a collection of empty islands. Up close, however, every island gave a volunteer a manageable section to complete.

Eventually,[4] Lina and I were assigned a band of pale tiles near the mural's lower edge. Maya's work gloves had orange stitching across the wrists.[5] Our section curved gradually, so we could not simply line the pieces in straight rows. Lina spread mortar over a small area, I pressed[6] tiles along the penciled arc. At first, I concentrated so narrowly on matching the line that I failed to notice the image taking shape around us.

[A] Sunlight reached the upper wall shortly after seven. [B] The silver tiles began reflecting thin streaks across the darker blue sections. [C] I stepped backward and recognized the outline of a river winding between buildings. [D] For the first time, I could see how our narrow curve belonged to the larger scene.[7] Maya handed Lina her cloth[8] so that Lina could wipe mortar from the tile faces before it dried.

By midmorning, the blank grid had become a bright map of the neighborhood; roofs, trees, tracks, and water[9]. Our names would not appear on the wall, and no viewer would know which pieces we had placed. That no longer bothered me. I had arrived believing that one person's handful of tiles could hardly matter. I left understanding that the image existed precisely because many people had finished one small section well.[10]
